newsitem.title: FRANCE: Franco-German alliance holds key to French policy.
newsitem.headline: Franco-German alliance holds key to French policy.

text.p: Whatever the result of France's parliamentary election on Sunday, the fundamental question remains the same -- how much can Paris shift policy without torpedoing shaky public support in Germany for monetary union?
That will be the key dilemma facing France's next prime minister, whether he be from the left or right.
In Paris, the political establishment remains deeply committed to launching a single currency on time in 1999.
"Respecting the deadline for European economic and monetary union appears as an absolute obligation," former European Commission president Jacques Delors said.

And though a first round election defeat for the centre-right is being seen here as a rejection of austerity, few yet believe France will put EMU at risk with a radical loosening of fiscal constraints which would damage German support.

Instead economists see a subtle shift towards a broader EMU, possibly with Italy on board, and an easing of policies which aimed to cut the budget deficit to precisely 3.0 percent of gross domestic product rather than somewhere near three.
"The question is not whether we go for EMU but how and under what conditions. There has been a common ground that 3.0 percent is a bit futile," Merrill Lynch economist Joanne Perez said.

But the new prime minister -- whether it be Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, Gaullist Philippe Seguin or liberal right-winger Edouard Balladur -- will be treading through a minefield in seeing how far France can go down the road to a broader EMU.

"There is still a chance it will cause a postponement," Eckhard Schulte, IBJ economist in Frankfurt, said. "It's very hard to sell the prospects of a broad EMU to the German population. We cannot be sure that Germany will play the game."
"The ball is going to be in the German camp," ABN Amro economist Philippe Brossard said. "The market wants to know whether Germany takes this opportunity to delay EMU," he said.

In Paris, the assumption is that Germany's decision to revalue its gold reserves to bolster its finances suggests it has softened its insistence on a strict interpretation of the Maastricht treaty and narrow membership for EMU in 1999.
"I was in Germany two weeks ago. I saw that the three percent blackmail was on the way out," Delors said in an interview with weekly Nouvel Observateur published on Tuesday.

"Germany has lost the moral high ground. There is room for there not to be a conflict (between France and Germany)," Perez said. "All this has left the market feeling that in one way or another we are going to get there (to EMU)."
But while Paris markets awaited Sunday's election result with remarkable calmness, German observers were less sanguine.

"Either a shift of government to the Socialists or a significantly reduced majority (for the right) will make it very hard to go ahead with fiscal consolidation," Juergen Pfister, head of economic research at Commerzbank in Frankfurt, said.
"If there is no further progress in consolidation it will be very hard to go ahead with EMU in 1999," he said.
According to Schulte, there may be subtle changes in Germany's attitude, as economic weakness makes it hard for it to fulfil a strict interpretation of the Maastricht treaty itself.

"Many people are becoming aware that Germany is no longer an outstanding country in terms of macro-economic performance," Schulte said. "Some people are going to understand that and that should take away some of that fear about a broad EMU".

"But it's going to be a very long way from there to the acceptance of a broad EMU," he said. "It will be very hard to explain giving away the mark for a currency which Italy is in. It is a barrier in the heads of the German people," he said.
Beyond the details of how EMU shapes up, there are other big differences in the way France and Germany perceive EMU.
In France, a single currency was debated in a 1992 referendum which produced a 51 percent vote in favour.

Since then, France has paid the price for its support with high interest rates to defend the franc and austerity. It would see delay as abondonment, rendering pointless the sacrifices of the previous years.
France also fears, far more than Germany, the threat to its economy of a devaluation of the Italian lira if EMU is either abandoned or goes ahead without Italy.
But in Germany, support for the euro in 1999 is in the minority and far fewer would see a delay as disastrous.
"In France there has really been a discussion. There has never been a discussion in Germany. Nobody fears disastrous consequences from a delay," Schulte said.
